name: English Final 5
description: EBRW FULL · 2 modules × 27 = 54, all original and extremely challenging (literature, science, and historical topics). Per module: 5 Words in Context + 3 Central Ideas & Details + 7 Command of Evidence + 7 Standard English Conventions + 3 Transitions + 2 Rhetorical Synthesis. Vocabulary drawn from the 550-word SAT list.

questions.passage: For much of the twentieth century, physiologists assumed that the adult human brain was essentially fixed—that once its circuitry matured, its structure was set for life. Studies of stroke patients who regained lost abilities, and of musicians whose years of practice reshaped the regions governing their hands, have overturned that assumption. The brain, it now appears, remains plastic well into old age, continually pruning unused connections and forging new ones in response to experience. What was once imagined as finished architecture is better understood as a perpetual construction site.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Musicians' brains differ structurally from those of nonmusicians because of the demands of practice.
Contrary to earlier assumptions, the adult human brain continues to reorganize itself throughout life.
Stroke patients rarely regain abilities they have lost, despite the brain's plasticity.
Twentieth-century physiologists contributed little to the modern understanding of the brain.

questions.passage: When the printing press spread through fifteenth-century Europe, its earliest products were not the pamphlets and newspapers we might expect but painstaking imitations of manuscripts: printers mimicked the handwriting of scribes, reproduced their abbreviations, and even left blank spaces for illuminators to fill in by hand. Only gradually did printers abandon these conventions and develop forms suited to the new medium. The revolution, in other words, at first disguised itself as continuity.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Early European printers initially designed their books to resemble handwritten manuscripts before developing distinctly printed forms.
The printing press was used primarily to produce pamphlets and newspapers in fifteenth-century Europe.
Illuminators refused to work alongside printers, slowing the adoption of the printing press.
Manuscripts produced by scribes were more elegant than the earliest products of the printing press.

questions.passage: Mr. Alden was not, by any measure the town used, a successful man. He owned nothing but the lamp he tended and the small rooms beneath it, and he had outlived whatever ambitions might once have drawn visitors to his door. Yet I have never met anyone who seemed so entirely the master of his hours. He rose when the light required him and slept when it did not, and in the long intervals between he read, and watched the water, and appeared to want for nothing that the water could not give.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's view of Mr. Alden?
options: She regrets that his early ambitions were never realized during his lifetime.
She believes his devotion to the lighthouse prevented him from forming friendships.
She admires the contentment he found in a life others would consider unsuccessful.
She is puzzled by his refusal to accept help from the townspeople.

questions.passage: Some plants release airborne chemical compounds when attacked by insects. The botanist Lorena Vasquez hypothesized that neighboring plants of the same species detect these compounds and, in response, preemptively increase their own production of defensive toxins before any insect reaches them.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Vasquez's hypothesis?
options: Undamaged plants positioned downwind of attacked plants showed elevated toxin levels, whereas equally distant plants upwind did not.
Plants under attack by insects released a greater volume of airborne compounds than undamaged plants did.
Insects were less likely to feed on plants that had already been damaged than on undamaged plants.
The defensive toxins produced by the plants were chemically distinct from the airborne compounds released during an attack.

questions.passage: Archaeologists discovered a cluster of 9,000-year-old dwellings whose floors were coated with a layer of white plaster. Because producing plaster requires heating limestone to high temperatures, one researcher concluded that the dwellings' inhabitants must have possessed kilns capable of sustained high heat.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researcher's conclusion?
options: The white plaster on the floors was noticeably thicker in some dwellings than in others.
No remnants of kilns have been found anywhere at the archaeological site.
Other settlements from the same period are known to have produced plaster using kilns.
The white coating was not plaster but a naturally occurring mineral deposit that forms without any heating.

questions.passage: The historian Amara Okonkwo has argued that a sharp rise in literacy in a certain nineteenth-century region was driven less by the founding of schools than by the spread of inexpensive printed almanacs, which gave ordinary people a daily, practical reason to read.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okonkwo's argument?
options: The almanacs contained not only calendars and weather predictions but also poems and short essays.
The number of schools in the region continued to increase throughout the nineteenth century.
In the region, literacy rates rose most steeply in districts where almanacs circulated widely but few schools had yet been established.
Almanacs were among the most commonly owned printed materials in the region during the period.

questions.passage: In an essay, a critic contends that the protagonist of a certain novel, though outwardly composed, is inwardly consumed by envy of his more accomplished brother.
questions.question: Which quotation from the novel would best support the critic's contention?
options: He congratulated his brother warmly, and only later, alone, did he find himself rearranging the trophies on his own shelf, as if their order could be made to matter.
"How well you have done," he said to his brother, and he meant it, for he had long since made his peace with the modesty of his own gifts.
The two brothers had quarreled as children, but the years had worn the old grievances smooth.
He rarely spoke of his brother at all, and when he did, it was with the distant courtesy one extends to a stranger.

questions.passage: Certain desert ants navigate by counting their steps, using an internal "pedometer" to gauge how far they have traveled from their nest. The zoologist Idris Farah proposed that if an ant's legs were experimentally lengthened after it left the nest, the ant would overshoot the nest on its return journey, because each step would now cover more ground than its pedometer assumed.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Farah's proposal?
options: Ants whose legs were shortened before an outbound trip took longer to reach their feeding site.
Ants deprived of visual landmarks were still able to return to the general vicinity of their nest.
Ants whose legs were lengthened after an outbound trip traveled past their nest before beginning to search for it.
Ants with lengthened legs walked more slowly than ants whose legs were unaltered.

questions.passage: In a clinical study, patients who took a newly developed drug reported less pain than patients who took an inert pill. The lead researcher concluded that the drug's active ingredient was responsible for the reduction in pain.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researcher's conclusion?
options: Patients who merely believed they were receiving a real drug reported less pain than those who believed they were receiving an inert pill, regardless of which they actually received.
Patients who took the new drug reported fewer side effects than patients who took the inert pill.
The new drug reduced pain more effectively than a drug already on the market.
Some patients who took the inert pill reported no change at all in their pain.

questions.passage: A guild in a medieval city required each prospective member to produce a "masterpiece"—a finished work demonstrating full command of the craft—before being admitted. The historian Bianca Reyes argued that this requirement functioned less to guarantee quality than to limit competition, by making admission slow and expensive.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Reyes's argument?
options: The masterpieces produced by applicants were often displayed publicly and admired for their craftsmanship.
Applicants who failed to produce an acceptable masterpiece were permitted to try again the following year.
The materials required to produce a masterpiece were costly and difficult to obtain.
The guild admitted far fewer new members in the years when demand for the craft's products—and existing members' profits—were greatest.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Zora Neale Hurston (1891–1960) was an American author and anthropologist.
  • She spent years collecting folklore across the American South and the Caribbean.
  • Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937) is her best-known novel.
  • The novel is set in Florida and written partly in the regional dialect of its characters.
  • Hurston's anthropological training informed her close attention to speech and storytelling.
questions.question: The student wants to explain how Hurston's anthropological work shaped her fiction. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Zora Neale Hurston, who lived from 1891 to 1960, was both an author and an anthropologist.
Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), Hurston's best-known novel, is set in Florida.
Hurston collected folklore across the American South and the Caribbean.
Drawing on the folklore and regional speech she had documented as an anthropologist, Hurston wrote Their Eyes Were Watching God partly in the dialect of the American South.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The tardigrade is a microscopic animal less than a millimeter long.
  • Tardigrades can enter a state called cryptobiosis, in which their metabolism nearly stops.
  • In cryptobiosis, they can survive extreme cold, heat, radiation, and even the vacuum of space.
  • A tardigrade in cryptobiosis can lose almost all of the water in its body.
  • Once conditions improve, the animal rehydrates and resumes normal activity.
questions.question: The student wants to explain how cryptobiosis allows tardigrades to survive extreme conditions. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The tardigrade, an animal less than a millimeter long, is microscopic.
Tardigrades are able to survive even the vacuum of space.
In cryptobiosis, a tardigrade's metabolism nearly stops.

By entering cryptobiosis—a state in which they lose nearly all their body water and their metabolism almost stops—tardigrades can endure extremes of temperature and radiation until conditions improve.

questions.passage: The second law of thermodynamics, which holds that the disorder of an isolated system tends to increase over time, has often been invoked to argue that the emergence of complex, highly ordered living things is somehow improbable or even anomalous. This reasoning misunderstands the law's scope. Living organisms are not isolated systems; they maintain their internal order precisely by increasing the disorder of their surroundings, radiating heat and excreting waste as they go. Far from violating the second law, life is among the universe's most efficient engines for obeying it.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Life does not contradict the second law of thermodynamics but is in fact a means of fulfilling it.
The emergence of complex living things violates the second law of thermodynamics.
Living organisms maintain their internal order without affecting their surroundings in any way.
The second law of thermodynamics applies only to systems that contain no living things.

questions.passage: The treaty was hailed at the time as a triumph of diplomacy, and by the narrow measure of its immediate aim—ending the war then being fought—it genuinely was. Yet the terms it imposed were so punitive that they impoverished the defeated nation and inflamed a resentment that would, within a single generation, help ignite a far larger and more terrible conflict. Whether a settlement deserves to be called successful, the episode suggests, may depend entirely on how long one is willing to wait before rendering the verdict.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The treaty failed even to achieve its immediate aim of ending the war then being fought.
The diplomats who negotiated the treaty were unaware that its terms were unusually punitive.
The larger conflict would almost certainly have erupted regardless of the treaty's terms.
Judgments about the treaty's success depend heavily on the length of the time frame one considers.

questions.passage: My uncle spoke of his early success as another man might speak of a debt. It had come to him young and easily, and he seemed to feel that everything he had painted since was owed against it—that the promise of those first canvases had placed him under an obligation he could never quite discharge. Praise embarrassed him; it reminded him only of the interest still accruing.
questions.question: Which choice best describes how the uncle regards his early success?
options: as an achievement he is quietly proud to have surpassed in his later work
as an accident of fortune that he believes he did not truly deserve
as a source of private comfort during periods of professional difficulty
as a burden that his subsequent work has never managed to repay

questions.passage: The paleontologist Nadia Sé proposed that a certain species of long-necked dinosaur held its neck roughly horizontal rather than raised. She reasoned that pumping blood all the way up to a vertically raised head would have required a heart far larger than the animal's body cavity could possibly have contained.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sé's proposal?
options: The dinosaur's nostrils were located near the very top of its skull.
Modern giraffes have unusually high blood pressure compared with other mammals.
The dinosaur's body cavity was somewhat larger than that of closely related species.
The dinosaur's fossilized neck vertebrae have joints that would have permitted only limited upward flexion.

questions.passage: A large study found that people who spend more time in green spaces such as parks tend to report better mental health. On the basis of this correlation, the researchers concluded that spending time in nature improves a person's mental health.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the researchers' conclusion?
options: Green spaces in wealthier neighborhoods tend to be better maintained than those in poorer ones.
People already in good mental health are more likely to feel able to leave their homes and visit green spaces in the first place.
People who exercise regularly report better mental health than people who do not.
The study measured time spent in green spaces using participants' own rough estimates.

questions.passage: A ledger kept by an eighteenth-century trading company records unusually high wages paid to its sailors during one particular five-year span. The economic historian Owen Brandt argued that these elevated wages reflect not the company's generosity but a severe labor shortage: so many sailors had been lost to disease and desertion that the company was forced to pay more simply to crew its ships at all.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brandt's argument?
options: The company's overall profits during the five-year span were higher than in any previous period.
Wages paid to sailors by rival trading companies remained stable throughout the same span.
The company's directors described themselves in private letters as fair and generous employers.
During the same five-year span, the company's ships frequently sat idle in port, unable to sail for lack of available crew.

questions.passage: In a work of criticism, a scholar argues that a certain poet, though widely celebrated for her serene nature imagery, encodes within that imagery a persistent anxiety about the passage of time.
questions.question: Which quotation from the poet's work would best support the scholar's argument?
options: The meadow lies unhurried in the sun, / content to be exactly what it is.
I love the brook's clear water, and the shade / the old oak lends the traveler at noon.
How green the hills, how wide and blue the sky, / how sweet the air that stirs the ripening wheat.
Each petal keeps its hour and then lets go; / the garden is a clock that blooms and dies.

questions.passage: Many migratory birds can sense Earth's magnetic field to orient themselves, but the mechanism remains debated. The biologist Tomas Reuben hypothesized that this magnetic sense depends on light entering the birds' eyes, where it activates a chemical reaction whose outcome varies with the bird's orientation relative to the field.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Reuben's hypothesis?
options: Birds were able to orient by the magnetic field equally well in bright daylight and in total darkness.
The magnetic field at the birds' breeding grounds was measurably stronger than at their wintering grounds.
Birds prevented from seeing, but otherwise unimpaired, lost the ability to orient by the magnetic field, while birds deprived only of their sense of smell retained it.
Birds with surgically damaged inner ears were unable to maintain level flight.

questions.passage: Observing that a certain coral reef recovered its coral cover remarkably quickly after a severe marine heatwave, a marine biologist concluded that the coral species making up the reef must be inherently resistant to heat stress.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the biologist's conclusion?
options: The heatwave raised local water temperatures higher than any previously recorded at the reef.
The corals that regrew after the heatwave belonged to a different, far more heat-tolerant species than most of those that had died.
Reefs in several other regions took much longer than this reef to recover from comparable heatwaves.
The reef supported a slightly greater diversity of fish after the heatwave than it had before.

questions.passage: The introduction of a new tax on windows in a certain country was followed by a marked decline in the average number of windows in newly built houses. A historian argued that builders were deliberately reducing the number of windows in order to lower their clients' tax burden.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's argument?
options: The window tax generated considerably less revenue than the government had projected it would.
Houses built in the months just before the tax took effect had, on average, substantially more windows than houses built in the months just after.
Windows were more expensive to install than equivalent stretches of solid wall even before the tax.
The tax applied only to houses above a certain total value.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek device recovered from a shipwreck in 1901.
  • It dates to roughly the second century BCE.
  • It consists of more than thirty precisely cut, interlocking bronze gears.
  • It was used to predict the positions of the Sun, Moon, and planets and the timing of eclipses.
  • No comparably complex geared device is known from anywhere in the following thousand years.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize the mechanism's sophistication relative to later technology. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a shipwreck in 1901, dates to roughly the second century BCE.
The Antikythera mechanism could predict the positions of the Sun, Moon, and planets.
With its more than thirty precisely interlocking bronze gears, the Antikythera mechanism was so sophisticated that no comparably complex geared device is known from the following thousand years.
The Antikythera mechanism was recovered from a shipwreck in the year 1901.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Honeybees communicate the location of food to one another using a 'waggle dance.'
  • The direction of the dance indicates the direction of the food relative to the Sun.
  • The duration of the waggle indicates the distance to the food.
  • The dance is performed in the dark interior of the hive.
  • Other bees follow the dancer closely, touching it to read the signal.
questions.question: The student wants to explain how the waggle dance conveys both the direction and the distance of a food source. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Honeybees perform the waggle dance in the dark interior of the hive.
Other bees follow the dancer closely and touch it in order to read the signal.
The waggle dance is one of the ways that honeybees communicate with one another.
In the waggle dance, the direction of the dance encodes the food's direction relative to the Sun, while the duration of the waggle encodes the food's distance.
